A presheaf on a topological space
Sections, restrictions, and global sections of a presheaf
Morphisms of presheaves
Separated presheaves
A sheaf on a topological space
A set-valued sheaf has a unique section over the empty open set
items.strategy: Apply the sheaf axiom to the empty cover of the empty open set. Existence gives a section, and uniqueness of the glued section forces any two such sections to coincide.

items.title: The sheaf axiom is the equalizer condition on a cover
items.strategy: A family of local sections lies in the equalizer exactly when the restrictions agree on pairwise overlaps. Gluing gives existence and uniqueness of a preimage, and the converse unpacks the equalizer statement back into locality and gluing.

items.title: The sheaf condition can be checked on a basis with basis-refinable intersections
items.strategy: Refine an arbitrary open cover by basis opens. Agreement on general overlaps is reduced to agreement on a basis cover of each overlap, so the basis sheaf condition reconstructs the full sheaf axiom; the reverse implication is immediate.

items.title: Presheaves and sheaves of groups, rings, and modules
Sheafhood of algebraic-structure valued presheaves is detected on underlying sets
items.strategy: The only extra data are operations respected by restriction. Once the underlying set-valued presheaf has unique gluing, the glued section is automatically the unique algebraic one because all structure maps are defined objectwise and commute with restriction.

items.title: The stalk of a presheaf at a point
Equality on a smaller neighbourhood defines the germ equivalence relation
items.strategy: Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. For transitivity, intersect the neighbourhoods witnessing the first and second equalities so that all three representatives agree on one smaller neighbourhood of the point.

items.title: Germs of sections
A section of a sheaf of groups is zero exactly when all of its germs are zero
items.strategy: If every germ of a section is zero, then near each point the section agrees with the zero section. These local equalities cover the domain, so uniqueness in the sheaf axiom forces the section itself to be zero.

items.title: Morphisms of sheaves are determined by their maps on stalks
items.strategy: Given two morphisms with the same stalk maps, their values on any section have the same germ at every point. Sheaf uniqueness then upgrades this pointwise equality of germs to equality of the two image sections.

items.title: A morphism of sheaves is an isomorphism exactly when it is an isomorphism on every stalk
items.strategy: Injectivity on stalks gives uniqueness of local lifts, while surjectivity on stalks produces local lifts around every point. The locally defined inverse maps agree on overlaps because their stalk maps agree, so they glue to a global inverse.

items.title: The etale space of a sheaf of sets
Sheaves of sets are equivalent to local homeomorphisms over the base space
items.strategy: Basic opens in the etale space are images of local sections, so the projection is locally a homeomorphism. Conversely, sections of a local homeomorphism glue uniquely on any open cover, and morphisms are recovered by how they act on the germs carried by those local sections.

items.title: The plus construction for a presheaf
The first plus construction is separated and preserves stalks
items.strategy: Two plus-sections that agree on a cover have the same germ at every point, hence coincide. Every stalk germ already has a representative on some neighbourhood, so the unit map to the first plus induces an isomorphism on stalks.

items.title: The second plus construction is a sheaf
items.strategy: After one plus step local uniqueness is available. A compatible family of first-plus sections can be represented locally by original sections, and the second plus step records precisely the data needed to glue those local representatives.

items.title: Sheafification of a presheaf
Sheafification is left adjoint to the inclusion of sheaves into presheaves
items.strategy: A map from the original presheaf into a sheaf sends compatible local data to compatible local data, so it extends first to the plus construction and then to the double plus. Uniqueness comes from the local-surjectivity built into the sheafification map.

items.title: Sheafification preserves stalks
items.strategy: Every germ of a sheafified section is represented by an original section on a smaller neighbourhood, giving surjectivity on stalks. Equality of two such germs is exactly eventual equality in the neighbourhood colimit, which is the original stalk relation.

items.title: Sheafification is idempotent
items.strategy: Apply the universal property to the unit map of a sheafified presheaf. Since the target is already a sheaf, the universal factorization supplies the required natural isomorphism.

items.title: Subsheaves
The image sheaf is the sheafification of the presheaf image
items.strategy: The objectwise image defines a subpresheaf of the target. Its sheafification maps into the target by the universal property, and this is exactly the smallest subsheaf through which the original morphism factors.

items.title: Classical algebraic prevarieties, regular maps, and varieties
Schemes as affine-locally locally ringed spaces
Affine open subschemes
Intersections of affine opens admit principal affine covers
items.strategy: Inside either affine open, refine the other open by distinguished opens; use the localization identification on each distinguished open and record the symmetric refinement. This proves the affine-cover comparison needed for every later local definition.

items.title: Gluing affine schemes along compatible open isomorphisms
items.strategy: Apply the established gluing theorem for locally ringed spaces to the open affine pieces and cocycle maps. Show that the resulting locally ringed space is affine-locally covered by the original pieces, then use the uniqueness clause to identify compatible maps out of the glued scheme.

items.title: Morphisms of schemes
Morphisms to an affine scheme and global sections
items.strategy: For a morphism to Spec A, take its map on global sections. Conversely, turn A to Gamma(X,O_X) into the canonical map X to Spec Gamma(X,O_X) followed by the affine map induced by A; verify the two constructions on affine opens and glue, then prove inverse naturality.

items.title: Morphisms of schemes are local on compatible open covers
items.strategy: Glue compatible locally ringed-space morphisms on a source cover, then use affine-open refinements of the target to check the local morphism condition. For equality, compare on a source cover and use uniqueness of glued maps.

items.title: Schemes and morphisms over a base scheme
Open immersions of schemes
Open immersions are monomorphisms
items.strategy: If two maps into the source have the same composite with an open immersion, their underlying maps agree because the immersion is injective onto an open subspace; restrict the inverse structure-sheaf map to obtain equality of locally ringed-space morphisms. Check closure under composition by composing the two open identifications.

items.title: Quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes
Affine schemes are quasi-separated
items.strategy: Cover a quasi-compact open in an affine scheme by finitely many principal opens. On a pair of affine opens, use the principal-open refinement lemma and finite basic-open covers to prove that their intersection is quasi-compact.

items.title: Ideal sheaves on a scheme
Quasi-coherent ideal sheaves
Closed immersions of schemes
Closed immersions into affine schemes are quotient spectra
items.strategy: Pull the defining ideal sheaf back to Spec A, identify its global ideal I, and use the affine anti-equivalence to identify the source with Spec(A/I). Conversely, the quotient map gives the required closed embedding and surjection of structure sheaves.

items.title: Quasi-coherent ideals and closed subschemes
items.strategy: State the mutually inverse assignments I to V(I) and Z to ker(O_X to i_*O_Z), checking on affine opens via quotient rings and compatibility on principal refinements. The general quasi-coherence proof is deliberately an AV-18 dependency, so this item must be authored as a source-backed recorded result rather than supplied with a local proof.

items.title: The reduction of a scheme
Universal property of scheme reduction
items.strategy: Check on affine opens that a map from a reduced coordinate ring annihilates the nilradical, hence factors uniquely through the reduced quotient. Use locality of morphisms and the affine-overlap lemma to glue these factorizations.

items.title: Irreducible components with reduced induced scheme structure
Integral schemes
Locally Noetherian and Noetherian schemes
Locally finite type and finite type morphisms
Locally finite presentation morphisms
Finite type is affine-local on source and target
items.strategy: Translate the condition to finite-type ring maps on affine charts. Localize generators for restriction, and for a finite affine source cover clear denominators and combine the finitely many displayed generators to recover the global affine criterion.

items.title: Quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphisms
Affine-overlap separation condition
items.strategy: For an S-scheme, record the affine-open criterion from Stacks Project, Schemes, Lemma 21.7: affine opens over a common affine base have affine intersection and the induced map on section rings tensored over Z is surjective. This is the self-contained separation interface used here; the diagonal formulation and the proof of equivalence are reserved for AV-14 after fibre products.

items.title: Scheme-theoretic varieties
items.strategy: Fix the convention that a k-variety is an integral, finite-type k-scheme satisfying the affine-overlap separation condition over k. By the source-backed affine criterion this is the usual separatedness condition, while the later AV-14 page supplies its diagonal formulation. This is a terminology interface, not a locally closed definition at this order.

items.title: Irreducible classical varieties and integral separated finite-type schemes
items.strategy: Let k be algebraically closed. Prove the equivalence between irreducible classical varieties, whose definition includes quasi-compactness or a finite affine cover, and integral separated finite-type k-schemes. Use Milne's closed-point functor from finite-type EGA schemes to ultraschemes and its quasi-inverse, which adjoins a point only for each nonsingleton irreducible closed subset, retaining each existing singleton point; on affine charts the established Nullstellensatz interface identifies the closed-point loci and their coordinate rings. Convert the finite classical affine cover to finite type and conversely use quasi-compactness of a finite-type scheme, while the closed/open lattice comparison preserves irreducibility and the affine-overlap interfaces match separatedness. Glue the compatible affine-chart comparisons and maps, without invoking the later diagonal formulation.

items.title: Scheme-theoretic image
items.strategy: For an arbitrary scheme morphism define its scheme-theoretic image, when it exists, as the smallest closed subscheme of the target through which the morphism factors; the following theorem supplies the quasi-compact existence and kernel description used on this page.

items.title: Scheme-theoretic image of a quasi-compact morphism
items.strategy: For a quasi-compact morphism, define the image ideal as the kernel of O_Y to f_*O_X, prove from quasi-compactness that this ideal is quasi-coherent and compatible with restriction to opens, and use the closed-subscheme correspondence. Verify minimality by factoring every competing closed subscheme chartwise; no quasi-separated hypothesis is required by Stacks Lemma 29.6.3.

items.title: A support does not determine its scheme structure

title: Schemes Subschemes and Morphisms Locally of Finite Type — Examples

items.title: The projective line from two affine charts
items.strategy: Glue two copies of Spec k[t] and Spec k[u] along D(t) and D(u) using u=t^{-1}; verify the cocycle is vacuous for two charts and identify the overlap coordinate rings.

items.title: The affine line with doubled origin
items.strategy: Glue two affine lines along their punctured principal opens. Compute its two origins and retain the construction as the later separatedness test case without using separatedness in this verification.

items.title: Two infinitesimal structures at the origin
items.strategy: For the ideals (t) and (t^2) in k[t], form the corresponding quotient spectra and compare their common support with their distinct coordinate rings.

items.title: Reduction of the dual-number point
items.strategy: Compute the nilradical of k[epsilon]/(epsilon^2), take the quotient, and identify the resulting one-point reduced scheme with Spec k.

items.title: A closed subset has many scheme structures
items.strategy: Use the family of ideals (t^n) in k[t] to obtain infinitely many quotient rings with the same vanishing set but different nilpotence orders, refuting determination by support.

items.title: Affine n-space over an arbitrary base
items.strategy: Define A^n_S by the polynomial algebra on every affine base chart and use the finite-type definition to check the structure map; include n=0 as the identity of S.

items.title: An infinite disjoint union is locally but not globally finite type
items.strategy: Take the infinite disjoint union of affine lines over a field. Each affine chart is finite type, while the inverse image of the one-point base has no finite affine subcover, so the structure map is not quasi-compact.

items.title: Finite type need not mean finite presentation
items.strategy: For a non-finitely generated ideal I of A, compare A to A/I: the quotient is generated by no new algebra elements but its kernel cannot be finitely generated. Translate this affine ring calculation to a morphism of schemes.

items.title: The scheme-theoretic image of a dense open immersion
items.strategy: For a dense open immersion into an integral scheme, prove minimality directly: on every nonempty affine target chart, any ideal defining a closed factorization restricts to zero on a dense open and hence is zero in the domain. Thus the smallest closed factorization is the whole target, without assuming the open immersion is quasi-compact.
